chunks: He said to the atheist when he asked him, 'What is He?' He said: 'He is a thing unlike all things. I reiterate through my words to establish a meaning: He is a thing in the true reality of thing-ness, except that He has no body, no form, cannot be sensed, cannot be touched, and cannot be perceived by the five senses. Imaginations cannot grasp Him, the passage of ages does not diminish Him, and time does not change Him.'

So the questioner said to him: 'Do you say that He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing?' He said: 'He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing — Hearing without an organ, and Seeing without an instrument. Rather, He hears by Himself and sees by Himself. My saying that He is All-Hearing who hears by Himself and All-Seeing who sees by Himself does not mean that He is one thing and the Self is another thing. I merely wanted an expression for myself, since I was being asked, and to make you understand, since you were asking. So I say: He is Hearing in all His totality — not that His totality has parts — but I wanted to make you understand and to express myself. My only reference in that is to the fact that He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware — without any difference in the Essence and without any difference in meaning.'

The questioner said to him: 'Then what is He?' Abu Abdillah, peace be upon him, said: 'He is the Lord, He is the Worshipped One, and He is Allah. My saying Allah does not mean affirming these letters — Alif, Lam, Ha — nor Ra, nor Ba. Rather, return to the meaning: a thing, the Creator of things and their Maker, and the attribute of these letters — and He is the meaning by which Allah, al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Aziz, and similar names of His are named. He is the Worshipped One, glorified and exalted.'

The questioner said to him: 'But we find nothing imaginable except a created thing.' Abu Abdillah, peace be upon him, said: 'If it were as you say, then monotheism (tawhid) would be lifted away from us, since we were not charged with anything other than what is imaginable. But we say: every imaginable thing perceivable by the senses is thereby limited and represented, so it is created. For denial is invalidation and non-existence, and the second way is tashbih (anthropomorphism).

The second is the resemblance (tashbih). Since resemblance is the quality of a creation that is manifestly composed and assembled — it was inevitable to affirm the Maker because of the existence of manufactured things and the compulsion that they are manufactured and that their Maker is other than them and is not like them. For if He were like them, He would have resembled them in the apparent composition and assembly, and in what applies to them of their origination after not having existed, their transformation from smallness to greatness, blackness to whiteness, strength to weakness, and their existing states — we have no need to interpret these, for their self-evidence and existence are clear.

The questioner said to him: 'But you have limited Him by affirming His existence.' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'I have not limited Him. I have affirmed Him — for there is no middle ground between negation and affirmation.' The questioner said to him: 'Does He then have a reality (inniyya) and a quiddity (maiyya)?' He said: 'Yes. A thing cannot be affirmed except with a reality and a quiddity.'

The questioner said to him: 'So does He have a how-ness (kayfiyya)?' He said: 'No, because kayfiyya is the aspect of qualification and encompassment. But it is inescapable to exit from the aspect of ta'til (negation of attributes) and tashbih (anthropomorphism): for whoever negates Him has denied Him, rejected His Lordship and invalidated it; and whoever resembles Him to something else has affirmed Him with the qualities of created, manufactured beings who do not deserve Lordship. But it is inescapable to affirm that He has a kayfiyya which no one other than Him deserves, in which nothing participates, which encompasses nothing, and which no one other than Him knows.'

The questioner said: 'Does He deal with things directly through His Self?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'He is more exalted than that things should come to Him through direct initiative and processing, for that is the quality of created beings — things only come to them through direct production and processing. But He is Transcendent, the Executor of Will and Volition, doing whatever He wills.'

key_terms.إِنِّيَّة: inniyya — 'that-ness' or reality; the affirmation that something exists (inna = 'indeed/verily', used here as the noun of existence)
key_terms.السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ الْعَالِمُ الْخَبِ: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware — four Divine Names affirmed in the conclusion
key_terms.الْأَوْهَام: imaginations/fantasies — the faculty of wahm (imagination), a term from Islamic faculty psychology denoting the estimative power that forms mental images of particulars
key_terms.تَشْبِيه: tashbih — anthropomorphism, resembling God to created things; the second error the Imam warns against
key_terms.تَعْطِيل: ta'til — stripping God of all attributes, leaving Him as an abstract void; one of the two errors the Imam warns against
key_terms.زِنْدِيق: atheist/dualist — in 2nd-century AH context, this refers to those influenced by Manicheanism or materialist philosophy who denied God or posited dualist creation
key_terms.شَيْئِيَّة: thing-ness — the philosophical property of being a thing; the Imam affirms God has true existence (shay') while denying He is like other things
key_terms.كَيْفِيَّة: kayfiyya — how-ness, qualitative state; the Imam denies God has a kayfiyya graspable by others, while affirming He has a unique kayfiyya unknowable to all
key_terms.مَائِيَّة: maiyya — quiddity, 'what-ness'; what a thing essentially is (from ma = 'what')
key_terms.نَافِذُ الْإِرَادَةِ وَالْمَشِيئَةِ: Executor of Will and Volition — describing God's absolute agency without physical mediation

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say when an atheist asked him 'What is God?' in the dialogue recorded in al-Kafi?
ai.summary: This hadith records the celebrated theological dialogue of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) with an atheist (zindiq), transmitted through Hisham ibn al-Hakam — the Imam's foremost student in kalam theology. The questioner pressed the Imam with a series of philosophical challenges about the nature of God: What is He? Is He truly Hearing and Seeing? Does affirming His existence limit Him? Does He have quiddity and quality? The Imam's responses articulate the via media of Shia theology: affirming God's existence and attributes while simultaneously denying any resemblance to creation (tashbih) or total negation of attributes (ta'til). God is 'a thing unlike things' — possessing existence, inniyya (reality), and maiyya (quiddity), yet free from body, form, sensory perception, and change. He hears and sees 'by His very Self,' not through instruments — and His Self is not divided into entity and attribute. The dialogue reflects the theological milieu of 2nd-century AH Iraq, where Mu'tazilite rationalism and Manichean/Zindiq challenges demanded rigorous philosophical responses. The Imam formulates a middle path between two errors: ta'til (stripping God of all attributes, leaving emptiness) and tashbih (anthropomorphism). This hadith was a foundational text for Shia kalam and was transmitted by Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who used these teachings in his famous public debates.
